blocks.x: I recently sent out a Slack poll to find out if and why my fellow staffers wear aprons at home, and the results led me to two conclusions: One, that many home cooks choose to go apron-free. Two, that those who do wear aprons do so in two primary scenarios: when doing messy tasks like frying (duh) and/or when having company over.

blocks.c: Image may contain Text and Page

blocks.x: To that end, the best apron should be durable and stain-resistant enough for everyday wear, but also chic enough to don for a dinner party, capable of both protecting and complementing your cutest outfit. I must attest that in my personal experience, owning a stylish apron also makes me more likely to reach for one before I start cooking, rather than as an afterthought once I’ve already stained my shirt.

What we love: I own five Hedley & Bennett aprons, which tells you most of what you need to know. The denim one is my grilling and pizza-making apron. It’s durable, and I never worry about staining it, since even red sauce and turmeric either wash out or disappear into the fabric. The cotton one feels substantial enough that I always feel well protected, and that’s my everyday pick. The cotton twill is lighter, so I reach for it when I’m washing dishes or doing something quick that won’t get messy.

The pockets earn their keep. A top pocket holds my instant-read thermometer, and the two on the bottom are big enough for my phone. Some people drape a kitchen towel over a shoulder or tuck it into the waistband, but I like having a dedicated towel loop. The neck strap adjusts, and the fit is flattering. I’m short, so I fold the apron over once at the waist, and it still looks sleek.
What we’d leave: Hedley & Bennett recommends hanging these to dry rather than tumbling them. That’s a small extra step, though it does preserve the fabric.

What we love: I added this apron to my collection two years ago, and it’s since become my most reached-for option (and I say that as someone who owns upwards of 10 aprons). I love the way the vibrant Sweet Pea color pops, that it’s made of sturdy 100% cotton canvas, and that it costs less than $60. But most of all I love the pockets. There are eight of them: three wide ones on the bottom and five slim ones on the top, which are perfect for holding tasting spoons, chopsticks, or plating tweezers if I’m feeling fancy.
The Cargo Crew also washes well. After two years of consistent use and many splatters and spills, my apron still looks good as new.
What we’d leave: While I believe it used to be available in more colors, the Boston Bibb style is only currently available in Distressed Denim, Rose Pink, and Sweet Pea.

blocks.c: wearing the cargo crew boston apron

blocks.x: Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior shopping editor

What we love: Since I started testing it out this has become my every day apron. The indigo denim looks gorgeous and hides stains incredibly well (not unlike some of the jeans I’ve loved and had to leave over the years); it’s also very lightweight, which I found a pleasant surprise. The pockets are useful; the two small ones at the top are good for holding things like cake testers or thermometers, the big ones lower down I use to hold my phone if I’m cooking from an app. Finally, considering that it isn’t a crossback apron, it doesn’t put any uncomfortable pressure on my neck.

What we’d leave: Gustin has a…different sort of production model. They crowdfund their all their production runs. I totally understand why that is safer than producing in large quantities you aren’t sure you can sell, but it does mean that a Gustin apron (or a pair of Gustin selvedge denim) isn’t always in stock. As I write this, the Selvedge apron is so snap it up while you can. If you miss it you’ll have to sign up to get notified when they produce another round.

What we love: I think it’s still pretty rare that a company focused on making one thing can sell quality pieces that are far removed from that thing. And in the case of Ooni, I’d say putting out textiles like aprons is pretty far from the pizza ovens that made the brand famous. But the pizzaiolo apron a tough canvas piece that holds up to more than a few stray tomato sauce spills. It’s thick, but still pliable and the large pockets can simultaneously accommodate tools like spoons, scrapers, and turners, and a phone if you’re using it as a cookbook. I also used the leather strap on the regular to hold a kitchen towel for cleaning smudges and cooktop spills.

What we’d leave: It pulls on the neck a little. Not so much that it bothers me, because I regularly use this style of apron as opposed to a smock or crossback (I think it’s a little easier to get on and off and hold in place), but I was aware of it while wearing. I think the utility of the rugged canvas more than makes up for that though.

What we love: I never really understood why someone would spend over $100 on an apron until I tried one from WhiteBark Workwear. The brand has been long beloved by professional chefs (including our own Chris Morocco) and it’s easy to see why: their aprons are made from butter-soft blend of organic hemp and cotton and are incredibly comfortable for all-day wear thanks to the cross-back strap design, which limits neck-pulling. Each apron has two deep lap pockets and two skinny chest pockets great for pens or small utensils, and long straps that are meant to be cut to your desired length. WhiteBack also offers complimentary hemming if your apron is too long.

The aprons are available in pretty much every color under the sun, but I went with French Indigo, a purple-tinged bright blue that brings me joy every time I put it on. I’ve been wearing mine nonstop since I got it, and have found that stains wash out with no issue.
What we’d leave: At $124 a pop, these aprons are a bit of an investment. That said, you really do get what you pay for when it comes to the look, feel, and durability.
